title: Scrape stuck-on debris off a griddle over the lip into its grease tray with a scraper
instruction: Scrape the griddle clean into the grease tray with the scraper.
context: Fast food cooks (O*NET 35-2011.00, about 670,000 US jobs, BLS) and restaurant cooks (35-2014.00, about 1.4 million) scrape the griddle between orders and at close. O*NET's tasks for fast food cooks include "Clean food preparation areas, cooking surfaces, and utensils" and "Operate large-volume cooking equipment, such as grills, deep-fat fryers, or griddles"; for restaurant cooks, "Inspect and clean food preparation areas, such as equipment, work surfaces, and serving areas". Food left on the heat while an order goes out burns onto the plate in separate stuck-on bits, and burnt food left there burns onto the next order. Each bit is stuck to the steel, so the scraper's edge has to be held flat on the plate and driven under it to break it free; a lifted edge rides over it. What it pushes spills round the blade's ends, so strokes have to overlap, and the pile has to be pushed over the lip into the tray, not flicked off onto the line.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. (1) Griddle: an Assure Parts 177AOGT1227 range-top add-on griddle (27 x 12-1/4 in. overall; a 22-3/8 x 12-1/4 in. (56.8 x 31.1 cm) cooking surface of 7-gauge type 430 stainless; 1-1/2 in. (3.8 cm) splash guards on both sides and the far end; a 3 x 12-1/4 x 1-1/4 in. grease tray across the open near end), set on the bench on its frame with the plate's top 5.0 cm above the bench and clamped down (fixed), tray end toward the robot, never heated (an equivalent plain steel plate of the same size, guards and tray serves as well). The plate runs from x 15.0 (the lip over the tray) to 71.8 and from y -17.55 to 13.55. The tray runs from x 7.4 to 15.0, its floor 3.2 cm below the plate's top. In real trials the plate is bare type 430 stainless, clean, dry and unoiled. The frame sits against two stop blocks on the bench (the plate's near right corner within 2 mm, the lip square within 0.5 degree, the plate's top 5.0 cm up within 2 mm and level). (2) Debris: 22 separate pieces of black Play-Doh (Hasbro), each 2.50 g (55.0 g in all), 1.9 cm square and 4.8 mm thick, pressed onto the plate, stuck to the steel where pressed and not to each other. Four rows 3.5 cm apart at x 17.5, 21.0, 24.5 and 28.0 (6, 5, 6 and 5 pieces, 3.5 cm apart along a row): y -10.75 to 6.75 in the 6-piece rows, -9.0 to 5.0 in the 5-piece rows. In the simulator each piece is a rigid body lying on the plate, bonded to it on its own by a breakable joint: it holds under its own weight and breaks free under the scraper's edge; once free it slides on the dry steel. The layout is the same every trial. Real trials (README, about 5 minutes, nothing heated): a fresh sealed 4 oz can is opened each trial (its lot code recorded); each piece is weighed on the scale to 2.50 g within 0.05 g and rolled into a ball, the 22 weighed together (55.00 g within 0.30 g); a foam-board template (Elmer's 3/16 in.) with 22 square 1.9 cm holes at those positions is laid on the plate, its near edge along the lip and its right edge against the right guard; each ball is pressed flat into its hole over parchment paper with the base of a measuring cup, a full 1 L water bottle (1 kg) standing on the cup for 3 seconds; the template is lifted. Contact check, by eye: every piece flat and fully in contact with the plate, with no lifted edges. The trial starts within 10 minutes. The robot's fingers wear fresh white nitrile glove covers every trial, so dough on a finger shows (README, Protecting the robot's hands). (3) Scraper: a Dexter-Russell Basics P94850 4 in. griddle scraper: stiff stainless blade 10.2 cm wide (1.5 mm thick in the simulator), 21.6 cm overall, white polypropylene handle 11.4 cm long (3.0 x 2.4 cm in the simulator) in line with the blade, 136 g. It lies loose on the bench right of the griddle, edge toward the robot, resting on its edge and the handle's end, centered at x 25.0, y -25.5 (in real trials laid in an outline traced on the bench, within 5 mm and 3 degrees). (4) Set-down square: a square of blue painter's tape (3/4 in.) on the bench, 12 cm on a side (outer edge), centered at x 25.0, y -40.0, right of the scraper; the scraper's start is 8.5 cm outside it. (5) Video: two phones film every real trial: one overhead (the whole plate, the scraper's outline and the taped square in frame) and one low at the plate's near left corner, looking along the lip. Both arms start at their ready pose. The trial runs at room temperature (20 to 24 degrees C), the same every trial.
scoring: Measured by mass, as shares of the debris (55.0 g, 22 pieces of 2.50 g), from where each piece ends up; the same definitions in the simulator and in real trials. Only the scraper may move the dough. A piece counts in the tray only if the held scraper's blade broke it free and pushed it over the lip, directly or through pieces the blade was pushing (in the simulator: the blade or its neck within 0.5 mm of the piece while the piece moves, the piece's first move made under the blade, and its trip over the lip within 0.5 s of such a push; the handle does not count). The robot touching any piece at any time (its own collision meshes, fingers to upper arm, within 1 mm while the piece moves) scores 0. In the tray means inside the tray's walls and below the plate's top. Off the griddle means outside its footprint (plate, tray and splash guards): on the bench, the floor, or on the scraper once it is set down. Everything else is left on the griddle. Dough on the scraper may be knocked into the tray before the set-down, for example by drawing the blade across the tray's rim; only what is on the blade at the set-down counts as off the griddle. 1.0: at least 98% credited in the tray and nothing left on the griddle (in the simulator every piece credited in the tray; each piece is 4.5%), and the scraper, after being picked up (held with its origin, where the neck meets the handle, 5 cm above where it lay), set down in the taped square, released and still for 1 s. Set down: that origin inside the square's outer edge and less than 3 cm above the bench; released: no gripper touching it; still: under 1 cm a second and 10 degrees a second. 0.75: at least 90% credited in the tray and at most 5% left on the griddle (one piece). 0.5: at least 60%. 0.25: at least 25% (about six pieces). Otherwise 0. Doing nothing scores 0. Two caps apply to every score. More than 5% off the griddle (more than one piece thrown onto the line) caps the score at 0.25. A gouge caps it at 0.5 for the rest of the trial: while the scraper is held and sliding with its edge on the plate (within 0.6 mm; 1.0 mm once a stroke has begun), the blade over 70 degrees to the plate, or its edge tilted over 10 degrees so only one corner touches, for 1 cm or more of a stroke. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. In a real trial the same shares are weighed on a BOMATA 0.01 g / 1 kg compact digital scale: the tray's gain (in the tray, T); every piece lifted off the plate, guards and blade over the griddle with a razor scraper (left on the griddle; a thin smear is not a piece); what is collected from the catch sheets, bench, floor and the set-down scraper (off the griddle). A trial whose total is more than 5% off the 22 weighed pieces is repeated. The two videos are watched back: each piece that reached the tray other than broken free and pushed over the lip by the held blade (or by pieces it was pushing) is counted, and 2.50 g is subtracted from T for each. A finger, palm or arm pushing, pinching or lifting any piece on the video, or dough on a white finger cover after the trial, scores 0. The pick-up and set-down are judged from the overhead video. Top photos before and after, under a fixed raking light with a 1 cm grid, record what is left; a new scratch in the steel 1 cm or longer is the gouge. Nothing left on the griddle means under 0.40 g left (under a sixth of one piece) and no piece 1 mm or larger on the plate, guards or blade (by eye under the raking light, against a steel rule and the grid photo).
reset_notes: About 3 minutes. Weigh the tray's gain, empty its contents into the waste bin (used dough is not reused), wipe the tray with a damp microfiber cloth and dry it. Lift anything left on the plate with the razor scraper, wipe the plate where the pieces were with a damp microfiber cloth (water only), then dry it with a paper towel, until the raking-light photo shows no particle 1 mm or larger and no smear. Wipe and dry the scraper's handle and blade. Fit fresh white nitrile glove covers on the robot's fingers and check the old ones for dough. Then make the next debris (about 5 minutes: fresh can, 22 pieces of 2.50 g, total 55.00 g, pressed through the template, contact check by eye, before photo). Clamp the griddle against its stops and lay the scraper in its outline. In simulation every trial starts with every piece bonded in place and the tray empty.
fidelity: Real size and mass: 22 pieces, 1.9 cm square, 4.8 mm thick, 2.50 g (55.0 g), sim and real. Each piece is bonded to the plate on its own: it holds under its own weight and breaks free under the scraper's edge; in real trials the same press sets the bond. Pieces are rigid in the sim; the score is by mass in both, so dough smeared or left on the steel counts as left on the griddle. Clean dry steel: 0.7 static, 0.6 sliding. No heat. Rigid scraper. Gouge: a blade-angle rule.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps); demo: 1.0 (2,169 steps, all 22 pieces credited). Both on task.py 766a5d174461.
